claim: New Caledonian crows in one study population use two types of stick tools: hooked and non-hooked.
source: NC crows in one of our study populations ('farmland' site in Rutz et al., 2012) use two different types of stick tools.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text with citation to prior work (Rutz et al., 2012).

claim: Non-hooked stick tools are twigs or leaf petioles sourced from the forest floor or branches removed from live vegetation.
source: Non-hooked stick tools (Figure 1a, top panel) are twigs or leaf petioles sourced from the forest floor, or branches removed from live vegetation (Hunt and Gray, 2002)
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Figure 1a and citation to Hunt and Gray, 2002.

claim: Non-hooked stick tools are ubiquitous, abundant, and usually require no modification before use.
source: they are ubiquitous, abundant, and usually require no modification before they can be used (Rutz and St Clair, 2012)
evidence: Directly stated with citation to Rutz and St Clair, 2012.

claim: Hooked stick tools are almost always made from the shrub Desmanthus virgatus.
source: Hooked stick tools (Figure 1a, bottom panel), on the other hand, are almost always made from one particular plant species, the shrub Desmanthus virgatus
evidence: Directly stated in text with reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Birds need to locate Desmanthus virgatus, select a suitable stem, and manufacture the hooked stick tool in an elaborate process including sculpting a hooked tip.
source: birds need to locate this patchily distributed material, select a suitable stem, and manufacture the tool in an elaborate process, including the careful 'sculpting' of a hooked tip (Hunt and Gray, 2004; Klump et al., 2015a; St Clair et al., 2016; Klump et al., 2019)
evidence: Stated in text with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Hooked stick tools require greater investment of time in search and manufacture behaviors than non-hooked stick tools.
source: it is evident that hooked stick tools will on average require a greater investment of time in both search and manufacture behaviours than non-hooked stick tools
evidence: Stated as evident based on the described differences in procurement processes.

claim: Self-manufactured hooked stick tools made from D. virgatus are much more efficient than non-hooked stick tools sourced from leaf litter.
source: we compared the foraging performance of crows using different tool types on standardised food extraction tasks and found that self-manufactured hooked stick tools made from D. virgatus were much more efficient than non-hooked stick tools sourced from leaf litter (St Clair et al., 2018)
evidence: Directly stated with citation to St Clair et al., 2018.

claim: NC crows prefer hooked stick tools over non-hooked stick tools when given a choice.
source: we predicted that NC crows would prefer these tools over non-hooked ones when given a choice
evidence: Stated as a prediction that was tested in the experiments.

claim: NC crows value hooked stick tools more highly than non-hooked stick tools, taking better care of them when not in active use.
source: we predicted that NC crows would prefer these tools over non-hooked ones when given a choice, and 'value' them more highly, taking better care of them when not in active use
evidence: Stated as a prediction tested in the experiments.

claim: Between 17 September and 28 November 2012, 24 August and 28 October 2013, and 5 August and 8 October 2015, a total of 64 NC crows were trapped.
source: Between 17 September and 28 November 2012, 24 August and 28 October 2013, and 5 August and 8 October 2015, a total of 64 NC crows (12 of them in more than 1 year) were trapped non-selectively with meat-baited whoosh nets in a farmland area near Bourail, on the central west coast of New Caledonia
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: 35 birds manufactured and used hooked stick tools and progressed to the main experiments.
source: In pre-testing sessions (for details, see St Clair and Rutz, 2013), 35 birds manufactured and used hooked stick tools and therefore progressed to the main experiments reported here
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: 27 birds participated in either one or both experiments.
source: Of these, 8 failed to interact with the task in their first trial, leaving 27 birds that participated in either one or both of our experiments
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: 23 birds participated in Experiment 1.
source: Twenty-three birds participated in Experiment 1 (5 in 2012, 9 in 2013, 10 in 2015; 1 adult female [CEO] was tested both in 2012 and 2013)
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: 17 birds participated in Experiment 2.
source: 17 birds participated in Experiment 2 (8 in 2012, 9 in 2013)
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: The sample of trapped birds was not significantly sex biased.
source: Based on these data, we conclude that neither the sample of trapped birds (binomial test: p=0.26, n = 64) nor the sample of subjects that contributed data to analyses for Experiment 1 and/or Experiment 2 (binomial test: p=0.08, n = 26) was significantly sex biased
evidence: Statistical test result reported in text.

claim: The sex and age composition of birds that contributed data did not differ significantly from that of birds that did not contribute data.
source: the sex and age composition of birds that contributed data did not differ significantly from that of birds that did not contribute data (Fisher's exact test for birds that contributed data vs. birds that did not contribute data; sex: p=0.20; age: p=0.56; see Supplementary file 1b)
evidence: Statistical test results reported in text.

claim: In Experiment 1, 21 tools were presented on a circular platform: 20 non-hooked stick tools and 1 hooked stick tool.
source: In each treatment, 21 tools were presented on a circular platform: 20 non-hooked stick tools and 1 hooked stick tool
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: The majority of tools were non-hooked to reduce the probability that crows would pick the hooked stick tool simply by chance.
source: The majority of tools were non-hooked to reduce the probability that crows would pick the hooked stick tool simply by chance.
evidence: Directly stated as the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: In Treatment 1.A, 1 hooked stick tool researcher-made from D. virgatus, 1 non-hooked stick tool researcher-made from D. virgatus, and 19 non-hooked sticks and leaf petioles sourced from leaf litter were presented.
source: In Treatment 1.A, we presented 1 hooked stick tool researcher-made from D. virgatus, 1 non-hooked stick tool researcher-made from D. virgatus, and 19 (non-hooked) sticks and leaf petioles sourced from leaf litter
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: In Treatment 1.B, 1 hooked stick tool researcher-made from D. virgatus, 1 leaf petiole, and 19 non-hooked stick tools researcher-made from D. virgatus were presented.
source: in Treatment 1.B, we presented 1 hooked stick tool researcher-made from D. virgatus, 1 (non-hooked) leaf petiole, and 19 non-hooked stick tools researcher-made from D. virgatus
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: In Experiment 2, Treatment 2.A provided 100 non-hooked sticks and leaf petioles of assorted length scattered on a material log.
source: one where the bird was provided with 100 non-hooked sticks and leaf petioles of assorted length scattered on a material log (Treatment 2.A)
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: In Experiment 2, Treatment 2.B provided 10 D. virgatus stems with several forked branches suitable for hooked stick tool manufacture.
source: a second, in which 10 D. virgatus stems with several forked branches (judged to be suitable for hooked stick tool manufacture) were presented wedged upright into the material log (Treatment 2.B)
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: In Experiment 2, Treatment 2.C provided three researcher-supplied non-hooked tools made from D. virgatus.
source: 8 of the subjects (all in 2012) participated in two additional treatments where three researcher-supplied tools made from D. virgatus, either non-hooked (Treatment 2.C)
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: In Experiment 2, Treatment 2.D provided three researcher-supplied hooked tools made from D. virgatus.
source: 8 of the subjects (all in 2012) participated in two additional treatments where three researcher-supplied tools made from D. virgatus, either non-hooked (Treatment 2.C) or hooked (Treatment 2.D), were presented on the material log
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: In Experiment 1, Treatment 1.A, almost all crows picked up, transported, and deployed the hooked stick tool and extracted the prey item with it (p<0.001, n = 15–17).
source: In Treatment 1.A, almost all crows picked up, transported, and deployed the hooked stick tool and extracted the prey item with it (p<0.001, n = 15–17; Figure 2)
evidence: Statistical result reported in text with reference to Figure 2.

claim: In Experiment 1, Treatment 1.B, crows significantly preferred the hooked stick tool for transport, deployment, and extraction (p<0.001, n = 9–12).
source: In Treatment 1.B, crows significantly preferred the hooked stick tool for transport, deployment, and extraction (p<0.001, n = 9–12)
evidence: Statistical result reported in text.

claim: In Experiment 1, Treatment 1.B, crows did not significantly prefer the hooked stick tool at the pick-up stage (p≈1, n = 12).
source: In Treatment 1.B, crows significantly preferred the hooked stick tool for transport, deployment, and extraction (p<0.001, n = 9–12), but not at the pick-up stage (p≈1, n = 12; Figure 2)
evidence: Statistical result reported in text with reference to Figure 2.

claim: In Treatment 1.B, fewer crows chose the hooked stick tool than in Treatment 1.A.
source: Interestingly, in Treatment 1.B (in which most non-hooked options were made from D. virgatus), fewer crows chose the hooked stick tool than in Treatment 1.A (in which most non-hooked options were leaf petioles) (Figure 2)
evidence: Observation reported in text with reference to Figure 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, crows kept their tools safe in 92% of 257 cases pooled across Treatments 2.A and 2.B.
source: In Experiment 2, crows kept their tools safe in the vast majority of cases (Figure 3), both in the two naturalistic treatments (92% of 257 cases, pooled across Treatments 2.A [non-hooked stick tools crow-sourced from leaf litter] and 2.B [hooked stick tools crow-manufactured from D. virgatus])
evidence: Statistical result reported in text with reference to Figure 3.

claim: In Experiment 2, crows kept their tools safe in 94% of 185 cases pooled across Treatments 2.C and 2.D.
source: the two additional treatments with researcher-supplied tools (94% of 185 cases, pooled across Treatments 2.C [non-hooked stick tools researcher-made from D. virgatus] and 2.D [hooked stick tools researcher-made from D. virgatus])
evidence: Statistical result reported in text.

claim: Subjects were significantly more likely to express safekeeping behaviour when foraging with hooked stick tools they had manufactured from D. virgatus (95% of 172 cases in Treatment 2.B) than when foraging with non-hooked stick tools they had sourced from leaf litter (87% of 85 cases in Treatment 2.A; model #1: GLMM: χ2 = 5.47, p=0.02, n = 257).
source: As predicted, subjects were significantly more likely to express safekeeping behaviour (storing tools underfoot or in holes) when foraging with hooked stick tools they had manufactured from D. virgatus (95% of 172 cases in Treatment 2.B) than when foraging with non-hooked stick tools they had sourced from leaf litter (87% of 85 cases in Treatment 2.A; model #1: GLMM [generalized linear mixed model]: χ2 = 5.47, p=0.02, n = 257; Figure 3)
evidence: Statistical result reported in text with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Crows stored hooked stick tools in holes more often than non-hooked stick tools (Treatments 2.B vs. 2.A; model #2: GLMM: χ2 = 19.78, p<0.001, n = 257).
source: they also stored hooked stick tools in holes more often than non-hooked stick tools (Treatments 2.B vs. 2.A; model #2: GLMM: χ2 = 19.78, p<0.001, n = 257; Figure 3)
evidence: Statistical result reported in text with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Tool type by itself did not significantly affect safekeeping behaviour (Treatments 2.C vs. 2.D; model #3: GLMM: χ2 = 1.04, p=0.31, n = 185).
source: The following factors by themselves did not significantly affect safekeeping behaviour: tool type (Treatments 2.C vs. 2.D; non-hooked stick tools researcher-made from D. virgatus vs. hooked stick tools researcher-made from D. virgatus; model #3: GLMM: χ2 = 1.04, p=0.31, n = 185)
evidence: Statistical result reported in text.

claim: Tool material by itself did not significantly affect safekeeping behaviour (Treatments 2.A vs. 2.C; model #7: GLMM: χ2 = 0.94, p=0.33, n = 142).
source: tool material (Treatments 2.A vs. 2.C; non-hooked stick tools crow-sourced from leaf litter vs. non-hooked stick tools researcher-made from D. virgatus; model #7: GLMM: χ2 = 0.94, p=0.33, n = 142)
evidence: Statistical result reported in text.

claim: Manufacture effort by itself did not significantly affect safekeeping behaviour (Treatments 2.B vs. 2.D; model #9: GLMM: χ2 = 0.06, p=0.81, n = 300).
source: manufacture effort (Treatments 2.B vs. 2.D; hooked stick tools crow-manufactured from D. virgatus vs. hooked stick tools researcher-made from D. virgatus; model #9: GLMM: χ2 = 0.06, p=0.81, n = 300)
evidence: Statistical result reported in text.

claim: Crows stored researcher-supplied hooked stick tools made from D. virgatus significantly more often in holes than researcher-supplied non-hooked stick tools made from D. virgatus (Treatments 2.D vs. 2.C; model #4: GLMM: χ2 = 7.24, p=0.007, n = 185).
source: Crows stored (supplied) hooked stick tools researcher-made from D. virgatus significantly more often in holes than (supplied) non-hooked stick tools researcher-made from D. virgatus (Treatments 2.D vs. 2.C; model #4: GLMM: χ2 = 7.24, p=0.007, n = 185)
evidence: Statistical result reported in text.

claim: Crows stored hooked stick tools self-manufactured from D. virgatus in holes more often than researcher-supplied non-hooked stick tools made from D. virgatus (Treatments 2.B vs. 2.C; model #6: GLMM: χ2 = 4.11, p=0.04, n = 229).
source: This increased tendency to store hooked tools in holes was also observed when comparing crows handling hooked stick tools self-manufactured from D. virgatus and (supplied) non-hooked stick tools researcher-made from D. virgatus (Treatments 2.B vs. 2.C; model #6: GLMM: χ2 = 4.11, p=0.04, n = 229)
evidence: Statistical result reported in text.

claim: The mode of safekeeping was not affected by tool material (Treatments 2.A vs. 2.C; model #8: GLMM: χ2 = 0.07, p=0.79, n = 142).
source: The mode of safekeeping (i.e., how tools were kept safe – specifically, whether or not they were stored in holes) was neither affected by tool material (Treatments 2.A vs. 2.C; non-hooked stick tools crow-sourced from leaf litter vs. non-hooked stick tools researcher-made from D. virgatus; model #8: GLMM: χ2 = 0.07, 0.79, n = 142)
evidence: Statistical result reported in text.

claim: The mode of safekeeping was not affected by manufacture effort (Treatments 2.B vs. 2.D; model #10: GLMM: χ2 = 0.03, p=0.86, n = 300).
source: nor manufacture effort (Treatments 2.B vs. 2.D; hooked stick tools crow-manufactured from D. virgatus vs. hooked stick tools researcher-made from D. virgatus; model #10: GLMM: χ2 = 0.03, p=0.86, n = 300)
evidence: Statistical result reported in text.

claim: NC crows strongly prefer hooked stick tools when they have access to both hooked and non-hooked stick tools.
source: In Experiment 1, we established that NC crows strongly prefer hooked stick tools when they have access to both hooked and non-hooked stick tools
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Experiment 1 results.

claim: NC crows are able to differentiate between hooked and non-hooked stick tools even when they are made from the same material.
source: they are able to differentiate between these tool types even when they are made from the same material (see also St Clair and Rutz, 2013)
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results with citation.

claim: Crows' preference for hooked stick tools was reflected in their tool-handling behaviour, with hooked stick tools being kept safe more frequently than non-hooked stick tools.
source: Importantly, Experiment 2 demonstrated that crows' preference for hooked stick tools was reflected in their tool-handling behaviour, with hooked stick tools being kept safe more frequently than non-hooked stick tools (Figure 3)
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Experiment 2 results with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Tool safekeeping has been observed anecdotally in otters.
source: Such tool 'safekeeping' has indeed been observed anecdotally in otters (Hall and Schaller, 1964)
evidence: Stated with citation to Hall and Schaller, 1964.

claim: Tool safekeeping has been observed anecdotally in chimpanzees.
source: Such tool 'safekeeping' has indeed been observed anecdotally in otters (Hall and Schaller, 1964), chimpanzees (Nishida and Hiraiwa, 1982)
evidence: Stated with citation to Nishida and Hiraiwa, 1982.

claim: Tool safekeeping has been observed anecdotally in Galapagos woodpecker finches.
source: Such tool 'safekeeping' has indeed been observed anecdotally in otters (Hall and Schaller, 1964), chimpanzees (Nishida and Hiraiwa, 1982), and Galapagos woodpecker finches (Tebbich et al., 2012)
evidence: Stated with citation to Tebbich et al., 2012.

claim: NC crows respond to an increase in tool recovery costs (foraging at height) with elevated levels of safekeeping behaviour.
source: Specifically, we have previously shown experimentally that NC crows respond to an increase in tool recovery costs (foraging at height) with elevated levels of safekeeping behaviour (Klump et al., 2015b)
evidence: Stated with citation to Klump et al., 2015b.

claim: Goffin's cockatoos respond to an increase in tool recovery costs with elevated levels of safekeeping behaviour.
source: a result that was subsequently replicated in Goffin's cockatoos (Auersperg et al., 2017)
evidence: Stated with citation to Auersperg et al., 2017.

claim: Goffin's cockatoos do not seem to routinely use tools in the wild.
source: a species that does not seem to routinely use tools in the wild (O'Hara et al., 2021)
evidence: Stated with citation to O'Hara et al., 2021.

claim: When NC crows' preferred safekeeping method of holding tools underfoot was made more challenging, they resorted to storing tools more frequently in holes.
source: Interestingly, when NC crows' preferred safekeeping method of holding tools underfoot was made more challenging, because subjects had to handle demanding prey before re-using their tools, they resorted to storing tools more frequently in holes, thereby preventing their accidental loss (Klump et al., 2015b)
evidence: Stated with citation to Klump et al., 2015b.

claim: The study is the first to use safekeeping behaviour as a proxy for assessing how non-human animals value different tool types.
source: To our knowledge, our study is the first to use safekeeping behaviour as a proxy for assessing how non-human animals value different tool types, establishing a novel paradigm for productive cross-taxonomic comparisons.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a novel contribution.

claim: The study establishes a novel paradigm for productive cross-taxonomic comparisons.
source: To our knowledge, our study is the first to use safekeeping behaviour as a proxy for assessing how non-human animals value different tool types, establishing a novel paradigm for productive cross-taxonomic comparisons.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a novel contribution.

claim: Crows altered their tool safekeeping behaviour in response to a combination of factors, including tool type and raw material.
source: Results from a series of control treatments suggested that crows altered their tool 'safekeeping' behaviour in response to a combination of factors, including tool type and raw material.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a conclusion from control treatments.

claim: The presence of a hook alone had a measurable effect on the mode of safekeeping.
source: Interestingly, closer inspection of the data revealed that the presence of the hook alone had a measurable effect on the mode of safekeeping (i.e., how, rather than whether, tools were kept safe).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from data analysis.

claim: NC crows pay attention to the presence of a hook, prioritising it over two other potentially efficiency-enhancing design features.
source: We had previously shown that, when presented with experimentally altered 'puzzle' tools (St Clair and Rutz, 2013), crows pay attention to the presence of a hook, prioritising it over two other, potentially efficiency-enhancing design features – a curved tool shaft and a functional end with bark removed (for discussion, see St Clair and Rutz, 2013; Sugasawa et al., 2017)
evidence: Stated with citations to St Clair and Rutz, 2013 and Sugasawa et al., 2017.

claim: NC crows sometimes employ a 'rule of thumb' when selecting tools, initially paying more attention to the tool material than to the tool type.
source: This could be an indication that NC crows sometimes employ a 'rule of thumb' when selecting tools (Hunt et al., 2006; Hunt, 2021), initially paying more attention to the tool material than to the tool type (see Klump et al., 2019 and discussion below)
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental results with citations.

claim: Non-hooked stick tools are apparently rarely made from D. virgatus in the wild.
source: While we have observed the manufacture of non-hooked stick tools from D. virgatus when birds are held in short-term captivity (and they appeared to treat these tools similarly to self-manufactured hooked stick tools; Klump et al., 2015b), non-hooked stick tools are apparently rarely made from D. virgatus in the wild (personal observation; St Clair et al., 2016)
evidence: Stated based on personal observation and citation to St Clair et al., 2016.

claim: Crows use co-occurring features as a cue for initially recognising and orienting hooked tools.
source: Crows certainly use co-occurring features as a cue for initially recognising and orienting hooked tools
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations.

claim: Subjects that picked up a hooked stick tool in the wrong orientation will usually re-orient it very quickly before use.
source: For example, subjects that picked up a hooked stick tool in the wrong orientation will usually re-orient it very quickly before use (St Clair and Rutz, 2013)
evidence: Stated with citation to St Clair and Rutz, 2013.

claim: There is considerable variation in the tool-making behaviour of wild NC crow populations.
source: More generally, it is known that there is considerable variation in the tool-making behaviour of wild NC crow populations (Hunt and Gray, 2003; St Clair et al., 2016; Steele et al., 2021)
evidence: Stated with citations to Hunt and Gray, 2003; St Clair et al., 2016; Steele et al., 2021.

claim: The Hawaiian crow is the only other known tool-using crow species.
source: to examine if the only other known tool-using crow species, the Hawaiian crow Corvus hawaiiensis (Rutz et al., 2016; Klump et al., 2018), exhibits similar safekeeping behaviour
evidence: Stated with citations to Rutz et al., 2016 and Klump et al., 2018.

claim: Tool material and design features can influence foraging efficiency.
source: Tool material (Lamon et al., 2018) and design features (Sanz et al., 2009; Sugasawa et al., 2017; St Clair et al., 2018) can influence foraging efficiency
evidence: Stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Tool material, design features, and transportation distance have been shown to affect tool selection.
source: both have been shown (together with transportation distance) to affect tool selection (Visalberghi et al., 2009; Sirianni et al., 2015; Luncz et al., 2016)
evidence: Stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: The selective storage and re-use of particularly efficient tool variants could contribute to the gradual cultural accumulation of technological innovations.
source: It also seems worth examining the possibility that the selective storage and re-use of particularly efficient tool variants could contribute to the gradual cultural accumulation of technological innovations – an extremely rare process that has only been suggested for two non-human species, NC crows and chimpanzees (Yamamoto et al., 2013; Boesch et al., 2020; Osiurak and Reynaud, 2020; Rutz and Hunt, 2020)
evidence: Stated as a possibility with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Cultural accumulation of technological innovations has only been suggested for two non-human species: NC crows and chimpanzees.
source: an extremely rare process that has only been suggested for two non-human species, NC crows and chimpanzees (Yamamoto et al., 2013; Boesch et al., 2020; Osiurak and Reynaud, 2020; Rutz and Hunt, 2020)
evidence: Stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Safekeeping behaviour provides a powerful proxy for the value of tools to their users.
source: Safekeeping behaviour provides a powerful proxy for the value of tools to their users, which can be studied productively with untrained subjects and allows for wide taxonomic comparisons.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the discussion.

claim: The safekeeping paradigm can be applied to untrained subjects and allows for wide taxonomic comparisons.
source: Safekeeping behaviour provides a powerful proxy for the value of tools to their users, which can be studied productively with untrained subjects and allows for wide taxonomic comparisons.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the discussion.

claim: The tool safekeeping behaviour of captive and wild NC crows has been previously shown to be very similar.
source: we consider it unproblematic that all our results were obtained in field aviaries as the tool safekeeping behaviour of captive and wild crows has been previously shown to be very similar (Klump et al., 2015b)
evidence: Stated with citation to Klump et al., 2015b.

claim: NC crows exclusively use non-hooked stick tools when extracting wood-boring beetle larvae from decaying candlenut logs.
source: Since crows exclusively use non-hooked stick tools when extracting wood-boring beetle larvae from decaying candlenut logs (Hunt, 2000; Bluff et al., 2010b)
evidence: Stated with citations to Hunt, 2000 and Bluff et al., 2010b.

claim: Crows 'value' hooked stick tools, which are both costlier to procure and more efficient to use, more than non-hooked stick tools.
source: These results suggest that crows 'value' hooked stick tools, which are both costlier to procure and more efficient to use, more than non-hooked stick tools.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion in the abstract.
